full_text_en:
Bookoo, Inc. v. Beijing Xuneng Network Co., Ltd. and TOM.COM LIMITED — dispute over infringement of exclusive right to use of works

Plaintiff: Bookoo, Inc. (hereafter Bookoo). Domicile: Fremont Central Boulevard, California, United States.

Legal Representative: Xu Bei, Chairman of the Board.

Agents ad litem: Gao Xueqing, Huo Ligang, Attorneys at Beijing Huizhong Law Firm.

Defendant: Beijing Xuneng Network Co., Ltd. (hereafter Xuneng). Domicile: Dongchang'an Street, Dongcheng District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Zhang Peiwei, Chairman of the Board.

Defendant: TOM.COM LIMITED (hereafter TOM). Domicile: Queen's Road Central, Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Legal Representative: Wang Xian, Chief Executive Officer and Executive Director.

Common agents ad litem for both defendants: Yu Mingyan, Attorney at Beijing Lutong United Law Firm; Hu Ronghui, Attorney at Beijing Zhonglun Jintong Law Firm.

Plaintiff Bookoo, Inc., having a dispute with defendants Beijing Xuneng Network Co., Ltd. and TOM.COM LIMITED over infringement of the exclusive right to use of works, filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court.

Plaintiff's Allegations: The defendants provided 26 works by writer Zhou Jieru to a website operated by defendant TOM for publication, thereby infringing upon the plaintiff's exclusive right to use the electronic versions of these works. The plaintiff requested the court to order the two defendants to immediately cease the infringement, publicly apologize, jointly compensate the plaintiff for economic losses of RMB 42,620, and bear the litigation costs.

Plaintiff Bookoo submitted to the court the following evidence: the text of the "Copyright License Contract" entered into between Bookoo and Zhou Jieru; the "Letter of Authorization" signed by Zhou Jieru on February 6, 2000; Notarial Certificates (2000) Jing Zheng Jing Zi No. 17185 and (2000) Jing Zheng Jing Zi No. 32341 issued by Beijing Notary Public Office, among other supporting documents.

Defendants' Defense: The works of Zhou Jieru involved in this case were published on the Today's Authors Net, and the TOM website merely provided links to web pages of Today's Authors Net. Such links were set up pursuant to a contract entered into between Xuneng and the competent authority of Today's Authors Net, namely Beijing Today's Viewpoint Cultural Affairs Development Center (hereafter Today's Viewpoint). The TOM website itself did not publish Zhou Jieru's works. Therefore, the acts of the two defendants did not constitute infringement, and the court should dismiss the plaintiff's claims.

Defendants Xuneng and TOM submitted the following evidence to the court:
1. The text of the "Literature Channel and Cultural Activities Cooperation Contract" entered into between Xuneng and Today's Viewpoint, to demonstrate the reason for setting up the links.
2. Notarial Certificate (2000) Chang Zheng Jing Nei Zi No. 04026, issued on December 18, 2000, by Chang'an Notary Public Office upon Xuneng's application for evidence preservation of the content related to Zhou Jieru's works on the TOM website. The notarial certificate confirmed that the web pages concerning Zhou Jieru's works all bore the notation "This column content is provided by Today's Authors Net." It also confirmed that when clicking on the titles of the works to view their content, the Uniform Resource Locator (URL) of Today's Authors Net was displayed at the bottom of each page, indicating that the works involved in this case were published on Today's Authors Net and that the TOM website obtained these pages through links to Today's Authors Net.

The Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court presided over the examination of evidence at trial. During the examination, the two defendants only expressed doubts about the authenticity of Zhou Jieru's signature on the "Copyright License Contract" and "Letter of Authorization" submitted by plaintiff Bookoo, but adduced no rebuttal evidence. This objection could not be sustained, and thus all evidence submitted by Bookoo could be used as a basis for determining the facts of this case. Bookoo objected to the evidence submitted by the two defendants showing that they only linked to, rather than published, the works, but also adduced no rebuttal evidence. This objection could not be sustained either. All evidence submitted by the two defendants could also be used as a basis for determining the facts of this case.

During the proceedings, upon the application of defendant Xuneng, the court requested Today's Viewpoint to provide explanations regarding the facts relevant to this case. Today's Viewpoint confirmed that Today's Authors Net was a website operated by it primarily for publishing literary works; the works of Zhou Jieru involved in this case had been published on the server of Today's Authors Net; the TOM website had set up links to Zhou Jieru's works on Today's Authors Net; and there was no explicit provision in the contract between the parties regarding such links. Xuneng inquired of Today's Viewpoint as to whether Today's Authors Net had the right to publish Zhou Jieru's works. Today's Viewpoint confirmed that Today's Authors Net had obtained authorization from Zhou Jieru to publish her works, but could no longer prove this fact.

Facts Found by the Court:

On December 1, 1999, plaintiff Bookoo entered into a "Copyright License Contract" with the author Zhou Jieru, which stipulated that Zhou Jieru granted Bookoo the exclusive worldwide right to use the electronic copyright of the licensed works for a period of six years from the date of signing. The licensed works listed in the contract included the two short story collections involved in this case: *Let's Do Something* and *Dancing with Long Sleeves*. On February 6, 2000, Zhou Jieru issued a Letter of Authorization to Bookoo, further clarifying the scope of authorization: "Bookoo, as the worldwide exclusive lawful licensee, solely owns and may use the electronic copyright of the authorized works. It may digitize the authorized works, and publish, reproduce, transmit, distribute, broadcast, and exhibit them in the form of electronic publications via disks, CDs, or the Internet, and may freely use the authorized works in electronic or digital forms, whether existing now or developed in the future due to technological advancement." In the Letter of Authorization, Zhou Jieru stated that she had not authorized any other third party.

On June 1, 2000, defendant Xuneng and Today's Viewpoint entered into a "Literature Channel and Cultural Activities Cooperation Contract," stipulating that the parties would cooperate in designing a literature channel for the website of Xuneng's affiliated company, producing relevant column content, and conducting related cultural activities. In the ancillary obligations clause of the contract, it was agreed that Xuneng and its holding company should prominently display on Xuneng's website's literature channel that the literature channel's cooperation partner was "Today's Authors Net" and create a link. Today's Viewpoint warranted that entering into and performing this contract would not constitute infringement or breach of contract against any third party, nor would it cause Xuneng or Xuneng's website to incur any liability to any third party due to entering into and performing this contract. The parties did not specify in the contract the specific works to be involved in the cooperation activities. The "affiliated company's website of Xuneng" or "Xuneng's website" referred to in the contract between Xuneng and Today's Viewpoint meant the TOM website operated by defendant TOM.

Pursuant to the cooperation contract, defendant Xuneng and Today's Viewpoint jointly established a Chinese Literature Channel on the simplified Chinese version (www.cn.tom.com) of the TOM website (www.tom.com) operated by defendant TOM. Within this channel, there was a column titled "Little Demon Zhou Jieru's Web," which contained the table of contents of the two story collections *Let's Do Something* (published by Zhuhai Publishing House) and *Dancing with Long Sleeves* (published by Huawen Publishing House). Below the table of contents page, it was marked: "The content of this column is provided by Today's Authors Net." Under the bibliography of *Let's Do Something*, there were titles of 12 short stories, including: *Speak by Lighting a Lamp*, *Extinguish the Lamp to Accompany*, *Fly*, *Fish*, *Chaos*, *Does It Hurt?*, *Let's Do Something*, *Lyric Age*, *Midnight Show*, *Premeditation*, *Fragrant Meat*, and *As Free as Divorce*. Under the bibliography of *Dancing with Long Sleeves*, there were titles of 16 short stories, including: *Don't Live Anymore*, *Live a Few More Days*, *A Smoke*, *Family Matters*, *Going to Nanjing*, *Memories of Being a Troubled Girl*, *Going to Changzhou*, *Look at Me, Looking at Me, Still Looking at Me*, *The West*, *Dancing with Long Sleeves*, *Xiao Lin and Xiao Lin's House*, *Keeping Company*, *Mei Lan, Mei Lan, I Love You*, *Twisted Neck*, *Making a Move*, and *Drowned City*. Visitors could read the content of the works by clicking on the titles of the works, except for *Does It Hurt?* and *As Free as Divorce*.

After discovering that the aforementioned works were being disseminated on the Internet through the TOM website, plaintiff Bookoo applied to Beijing Notary Public Office on July 12, 2000, for evidence preservation of the relevant content on the TOM website, and again on October 19, 2000, for evidence preservation of the relevant content capable of proving the subject status of the website operator on the TOM website.

It was also found that in July 2000, plaintiff Bookoo had asserted its rights by email to Today's Authors Net regarding the publication of Zhou Jieru's works, but defendants Xuneng and TOM were unaware of this action. Upon learning of the lawsuit filed by Bookoo, Xuneng immediately conducted evidence preservation of the content related to Zhou Jieru's works on the TOM website. After Xuneng completed the evidence preservation, the TOM website immediately terminated the link with Today's Authors Net. Bookoo admitted that it had not asserted its rights to Xuneng or TOM before filing the lawsuit.

The above facts are confirmed by the evidence submitted by both parties, the certificate issued by Today's Viewpoint, and the statements made by both parties in court.

Opinion of the Court:

Plaintiff Bookoo obtained the exclusive right to use the electronic versions of Zhou Jieru's works by entering into the Copyright License Contract. Currently, China's laws do not have specific provisions on how to protect copyright in the Internet environment or on the obligations of persons involved when linking gives rise to copyright issues. However, in accordance with the legislative spirit of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, the legitimate rights and interests of copyright holders must be protected even in the Internet environment, and the works of others may not be used without authorization. In handling copyright disputes arising in the Internet environment, the principle of reasonably balancing the rights and obligations of both parties should be followed.

The website operated by defendant TOM, through the authorization granted by the contract between defendant Xuneng and Today's Viewpoint, linked to the web pages containing Zhou Jieru's works published on Today's Authors Net. The key issue in dispute between the parties in this case concerning the copyright dispute arising from such authorized linking is whether the link-setter bears legal liability.

Linking, as a technical means to facilitate visitors' access to information on the Internet, is currently widely used by website operators. From a technical perspective, the function of a link is to guide the visitor's browser to visit the website that uploaded the linked content. Where links are set between websites, although Internet visitors see the content disseminated online through the link-setter, such linked content is not "reproduced" and uploaded to the network by the link-setter, nor does the link-setter store such content on its own server. From the perspective of using the work, in the Internet environment, only the website that uploads the work to its server and then to the network is the user of the work. Setting a link does not directly use the work nor directly disseminate the work; it merely provides visitors with a convenient means to browse existing content on the Internet while simultaneously helping the website that uploaded the work to disseminate it. Therefore, the link-setter is not the user of the work.

Plaintiff Bookoo's principal argument in alleging that defendants Xuneng and TOM infringed its exclusive right of use was that, since Xuneng had entered into a cooperation agreement with Today's Viewpoint to jointly provide website content for TOM's website and authorized TOM's website to link to Today's Authors Net, Xuneng and TOM should bear a duty to examine in advance the content of the linked web pages. Their failure to fulfill this duty resulted in the illegal dissemination of the works, and they had subjective fault with respect to the occurrence of the infringement, thus they should bear liability.

Currently, it is precisely because of the widespread linking relationships between websites that the Internet can rapidly disseminate a vast amount of various information. If link-setters were required to bear a duty of prior examination of the linked content when setting links, this would undoubtedly impede the function of linking, which would be detrimental to the development of the Internet industry. At the same time, it should be recognized that link-setters set links in order to increase the traffic of their own websites and to obtain greater economic benefits. While benefiting, link-setters should, in accordance with the principle of equality between rights and obligations, exercise due diligence with respect to whether setting links would prejudice the exercise of rights by others.

In the case of authorized linking, whether the link-setter bears liability can be divided into two scenarios: If the link-setter knows that the linked work has a defect in rights and nonetheless provides the link, its conduct undoubtedly assists the infringer in dissemination and expands the infringement results. In such a case, both the website that uploaded the work and the link-setter should bear tort liability. If the link-setter did not know in advance that the linked work had a defect in rights and provided the link, it has no subjective intent to infringe and naturally does not need to bear civil liability; such liability can only be borne by the website that uploaded the work. The cooperation contract between defendant Xuneng and Today's Viewpoint only stipulated cooperation in designing a literature channel for the TOM website, producing relevant column content, and conducting related cultural activities, with the TOM website linking to Today's Authors Net to obtain the column content. It did not specify which works would be used in the columns. Therefore, Xuneng and TOM could not know before setting the link that the linked works had a defect in rights. When signing the contract, Xuneng was aware that disseminating others' works through linking might involve the protection of the rights of the work's right holders, and therefore, at the time of contracting, it demanded clear guarantees of rights from the other party, thereby exercising appropriate due diligence. There was no common intention between Xuneng and TOM and the website that uploaded the works to disseminate the works that infringed plaintiff Bookoo's exclusive right of use. After Bookoo filed the lawsuit, when Xuneng and TOM learned that the link was prejudicing the exercise of another's rights, they promptly severed the link. Therefore, Xuneng and TOM did not commit any act of infringement and should not bear civil liability for infringement. Bookoo's claim that Xuneng and TOM infringed its rights is unfounded, and its request for relief is not supported.

In conclusion, the Beijing No. 2 Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on April 27, 2001:

Judgment:

The claims of plaintiff Bookoo, Inc., are dismissed.

The case acceptance fee of RMB 1,706 shall be borne by plaintiff Bookoo, Inc.

After the judgment was announced, neither party appealed, and the first-instance judgment became legally effective.
